page7_img_1.png.title: Normalized casts vs. parameterized types over time (eclipse-cs, jedit, squirrel-sql)
page7_img_1.png.description: Three side-by-side time-series plots (years ~2000–2009) compare the normalized number of casts (red, top line) with normalized parameterized-type uses (blue, bottom line; multiplied by 10 to make it visible) for eclipse-cs, jedit, and squirrel-sql. In eclipse-cs the cast rate spikes around 2003–2004 then settles at a lower level while parameterized types remain near zero until a sharp rise around 2007–2008. In jedit casts decline from the early 2000s and remain relatively steady thereafter while parameterized types grow gradually from about 2004 onward. In squirrel-sql a pronounced jump in parameterized types in 2007 coincides with a clear drop in casts, illustrating one of the stronger inverse relationships between generics adoption and casts shown in the paper. The y‑values are ratios normalized by Halstead program length (blue series scaled by ×10).

page5_img_1.png.title: Most common parameterized types in Squirrel‑SQL (counts)
page5_img_1.png.description: A ranked table of the most frequent parameterized types found in the Squirrel‑SQL codebase, with occurrence counts (top entries shown): List<String> 1066, ArrayList<String> 682, HashMap<String,String> 554, List<ObjectTreeNode> 376, List<ITableInfo> 322, Class<?> 314, List<TableColumnInfo> 304, Vector<String> 234, List<ArtifactStatus> 196, Collection<String[]> 166, List<Object[]> 132, Iterator<String> 124, ArrayList<MappedClassInfo> 114, Set<String> 102. The list is dominated by collection types (many List/ArrayList/Vector/Collection/Iterator/Set) and String is the most common type argument. These counts corroborate the paper’s observation that generics are used primarily for type‑safe collections—Lists (especially Lists of String) are the single largest category of parameterizations in this project.

page8_img_1.png.title: Raw vs. Parameterized Type Usage Over Time in Squirrel‑SQL, Eclipse‑cs, and JEdit
page8_img_1.png.description: Three time-series plots (x-axis: date; y-axis: number of type uses) compare raw types (solid red lines) to parameterized/generic types (dashed blue lines) for Squirrel‑SQL, Eclipse‑cs, and JEdit. Squirrel‑SQL shows a rapid migration around 2007: parameterized types jump from near zero to well over 2,000 by 2010 while raw types drop from ~1,200 to ~700 (the paper reports 574 of 1,411 raw types, 40.7%, were converted during this period). Eclipse‑cs delays adoption until ~2008, when parameterized types rise to about 280–300 but raw types remain near ~400–450 (only 30 of 497 raw types, ~6%, were converted). JEdit exhibits earlier raw‑type growth (peaking ~3,000) and a later steep increase in parameterized types after 2006 that by 2010 overtakes raw usage; overall conversion in JEdit was modest (517 of 4,360 raw types, ~11.9%). These plots illustrate that when projects adopt generics the change is often concentrated in short periods and that complete migration of legacy raw types is uncommon.

page5_img_2.png.title: Raw vs. parameterized type counts across 20 Java projects
page5_img_2.png.description: Stacked vertical bars compare counts of raw types (gray) and parameterized/generic types (blue) for each of the 20 studied projects; the y‑axis is labeled “# Raw and Generic Types (thousands)” and a legend shows gray=raw, blue=parameterized. The chart shows that raw (non‑generic) uses dominate in most projects, with Eclipse JDT and Spring having the largest totals overall while the blue parameterized portion is relatively small for many projects. A small subset of projects (for example maven3, jedit, commons‑collections, lucene, and squirrel‑sql) exhibit visibly larger blue segments, indicating more substantial use of parameterized types there. This visualizes the paper’s finding that generics were used unevenly across projects and that, where used, they often represent only a fraction of the total opportunities for generification.

page9_img_1.png.title: Contributor-level raw vs parameterized type introductions over time (Squirrel‑SQL, Eclipse‑cs, JEdit)
page9_img_1.png.description: Three time-series subplots (Squirrel‑SQL, Eclipse‑cs, JEdit) plot type introductions/removals on the y‑axis against date on the x‑axis; solid lines are raw types (candidates for generification) and dashed lines are parameterized (generic) types, with each color showing one of the five most active contributors. Squirrel‑SQL shows a single contributor producing a sharp rise in parameterized types around 2007 (dashed red climbs to roughly 2,500) with a concurrent drop in that contributor’s raw types—consistent with the paper’s finding of a concentrated generification effort (574 raw types converted over a five‑month period). Eclipse‑cs exhibits a similar single‑champion pattern: one contributor’s dashed line jumps near 2008 to about 300 parameterizations while overall project conversion was small (30 of 497 raw types). By contrast JEdit shows multiple contributors beginning to add parameterized types around 2006–2008 (several dashed lines rise to hundreds or over a thousand), illustrating a more collective adoption; overall the figure supports the paper’s conclusion that generics are usually championed by one or two developers, with exceptions like JEdit.
